title: Six Degrees from Nebraska to Boston
text:
How many acquaintances separate any two people in a large country? In the 1960s Stanley Milgram, then at Harvard, set out to measure it. The 1969 paper with Jeffrey Travers describes the best known version.

Nearly three hundred people received a folder about the study. Most lived in Nebraska; the rest lived in the Boston area. Each was given the name and some details of a target person, a stockbroker who lived in Sharon, Massachusetts, and worked in Boston. The rule was simple: if you know the target personally, send him the folder. If not, send it to a friend or acquaintance you know on a first-name basis who is more likely to know him. Each person who forwarded the folder also mailed a postcard to the researchers, so they could trace the chain.

Most chains died out along the way. But 64 folders reached the stockbroker, and those that arrived had passed through a strikingly short number of hands: about five intermediaries on average. Many of the final steps passed through a few well-connected people who knew the target. The result gave rise to the phrase "six degrees of separation," and to the idea that even a huge society is a small world.
lesson: You are only a few introductions away from almost anyone. When you need to reach someone, ask the people you know who they know.
source: Travers, J., and Milgram, S. (1969). An experimental study of the small world problem. Sociometry, 32(4), 425-443.
caveat: Most chains never reached the target, and critics have argued that the average was based on a small and possibly unrepresentative set of completed chains.
